study.title: Acts 7 - Stephen's speech: promise, rejection, and testimony to death
study.overview: Acts 7 presents Stephen's defense before the council, but the speech quickly becomes an accusatory testimony against the spiritual hardness of the people themselves. Instead of defending himself only from the accusation of blasphemy, Stephen recalls Israel's story to show a repeated pattern: God calls, leads and delivers; but the people often reject the envoys of God, resist his word and cling to external signs without obeying from heart. The chapter culminates in Stephen's martyrdom, the end of which resembles that of Jesus: he sees the glory of God, confesses the exaltation of Christ and prays for his aggressors.

outline.title: Abraham, Joseph and God's faithfulness in the formation of the people
outline.explanation: Stephen begins with Abraham, called when he was still outside the promised land, to show that the initiative of the covenant came from God and not from human privileges. Then he passes through Joseph, rejected by the brothers, but supported by God until he is an instrument of preservation of the family. History shows that the divine promise advances even when the patriarchs themselves act with envy, rejection and blindness.

outline.title: Moses, rejection of the deliverer and the God who sees affliction
outline.explanation: The second part highlights Israel's growth in Egypt, oppression under a new king and the birth of Moses. Although Moses acted zealously by the brethren, he was rejected at the first moment. Even so, God called him in the desert, revealed his holiness and promised deliverance, showing that deliverance comes on divine initiative and through the agent chosen by God.

outline.title: Moses, the desert, idolatry, and the limit of the temple
outline.explanation: Stephen identifies Moses as the leader and deliverer rejected, but sent by God, and connects him to the promise of a prophet like him, to whom the people should hear. Then recall the rebellion in the desert, the making of the calf and the continuity of the tabernacle to the temple of Solomon. The argument reaches its high point by stating that the Most High is not attached to buildings made by human hands.

outline.title: Final Accusation, Vision of Jesus and Death Forgiving
outline.explanation: Stephen applies history to the present: the counsel resists the Holy Spirit, pursues the prophets and rejects the Righteous. The reaction is of fury, but he, full of the Spirit, sees Jesus at the right hand of God and declares the vision. His martyrdom ends with prayer for forgiveness to the murderers, mirroring Jesus' posture on the cross.

study.context: The chapter occurs in the context of a religious trial against Stephen, accused of speaking against Moses, the law, and the temple. The notes highlight that his speech is not a simple autobiography or an escape from the theme, but a prophetic response: he recalls the history of Israel to expose the recurrence of rejection to God's envoys. It is also relevant that the text presents it as the first martyr of the Christian church, so that his death functions as a paradigm of faithful witness under persecution.
study.theology: Acts 7 teaches that the history of salvation is conducted by God's sovereign initiative, not by the merit of the people. The promise made to Abraham advances through unexpected choices, suffering and deliverance; Joseph and Moses are examples of sent rejected before they are recognized. The chapter also affirms the centrality of inner obedience: circumcision, temple and law are not enough when the heart resists the Holy Spirit. The true guilt of Israel, according to Stephen's speech, is not only ritual or institutional, but spiritual and moral: rejecting the Justus, persecuting the prophets and disobeying the law received. At the same time, the text opens space for the Christian reading of Jesus as the promised prophet and as the Son of man exalted at the right hand of God. Finally, Stephen's martyrdom shows that the disciple participates in the way of the Master: suffering, a vision of divine glory, confident surrender of life and intercession by enemies.

scholarViews.insight: Stephen's speech turns his defense into a divine accusation against the obstinacy of the people, recalling the repeated rejection of God's envoys throughout Israel's history.
Joseph's account shows that God was with him and exalted him despite the envy of the brothers, showing that divine providence leads history even through human rejection.
The statement about the fulfillment of the time of promise shows Israel's extraordinary growth in Egypt as the work of God's providence, which makes a family become a nation.

questions: What similarities exist between the rejection of Joseph, Moses and Jesus, and how does this confront the way we treat God's envoys today?
In what situations can we be valuing external signs of religiosity, such as temple, tradition or position, but resisting the Holy Spirit of heart?
How does Stephen's prayer for his murderers challenge our practice of forgiveness in the face of real offenses?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a spiritual mirror: Ask God to show where you resist your word by habit, pride or attachment to external forms of religion. Then choose a concrete attitude of inner obedience this week: to reconcile with someone, to abandon a practice of hardness, or to intercede for someone who hurt him. It is also worth contemplating Stephen's posture as a model of fidelity: to speak the truth without aggression, to suffer without bitterness and to give his life to Jesus with confidence.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are selective and do not comment each verse of the chapter, so some transitions and applications were synthesized from the biblical text itself. There is also a possible textual tension in 7:16 on the reference of the grave in Shechem, but the notes do not clarify this issue, so I did not develop it as a firm conclusion.
